articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova later caleld the Tycho supernova with his bare eyes. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

articles.title: I Still Feel Like a Fraud. Here's What Actually Helps.
articles.excerpt: I keep waiting for it to go away. Every new skill, every finished project, every piece of positive feedback I expect it to be the thing that finally makes me feel like I actually know what I'm doing.…
articles.body: I keep waiting for it to go away. Every new skill, every finished project, every piece of positive feedback I expect it to be the thing that finally makes me feel like I actually know what I'm doing. It never fully does. The gap between what I know and what I feel On paper, things are going well. I'm building real projects. I'm writing about what I learn. People are reading, commenting, engaging. I'm gaining actual experience, not just theoretical knowledge. And yet there's still this quiet voice that shows up every time I start something new. "What if this time it's obvious you don't actually know what you're doing?" It doesn't matter how many times I've proven that voice wrong. It shows up again at the next challenge, as if none of the previous ones counted.

articles.body: Your agent works for twenty minutes. You are in another window. It tells you what happened — in its own words, in eight seconds. The first time it happened I was reading something else. The machine had been quiet for a while, then it said: "Tests are green, forty two of forty two. Next I'm taking the API layer." I stopped and listened. Then I went back to what I was doing, and for the first time in a long session I was not refreshing a tab every two minutes. That is the whole product. The rest is plumbing. The wrong unit Agent voice usually means one of two things. Either the final answer gets read aloud, which is useless while you are away, or a chime plays when the run ends, which tells you that something happened but not what. Both treat speech as a notification channel for text.

articles.title: Openfire exposure needs an admin-console and TLS boundary review
articles.excerpt: Openfire exposure needs an admin-console and TLS boundary review Openfire is an XMPP server with an administration console and configurable TLS support. The admin console is not the same service as cl…
articles.body: Openfire exposure needs an admin-console and TLS boundary review Openfire is an XMPP server with an administration console and configurable TLS support. The admin console is not the same service as client messaging, and each path has its own certificate and access expectations. An internet inventory should distinguish the two before an operator treats a host as safely exposed or safely internal. Openfire's installation guide says administrators can open TCP 9090 and 9091 for remote administration, and it identifies the resources/security directory as the location for keystores used for SSL connection security [1].

articles.title: What's that bright 'star' in the early morning sky? It's not a star at all!
articles.excerpt: Spotted a dazzling light in the eastern sky before sunrise? It's Venus, and the planet is only going to get brighter as it heads toward its spectacular peak later this month.
articles.body: Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!" The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky.

articles.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
articles.excerpt: The Andromeda galaxy is one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye. The difficult part isn't finding it. It's believing that faint smudge really is another galaxy.
articles.body: The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened.

articles.body: Someone at the White House appears to be running software that could enable outsiders to rent access on the presidential network for just "a few dollars," as reported by Krebs on Security and The Register . That's according to findings from the security firms Layer3 Intel and Synthient , which discovered residential proxy activity on the White House network. A residential proxy opens up a way for people to rent access to a home IP address and route their internet traffic through it, allowing them to conceal where their activity is actually coming from.
